ledeLeadHtml: Japan's most logistics-pure warehouse major, repriced by a capital reset
ledeHtml: Mitsui-Soko Holdings (9302) is the holding company of the Mitsui-Soko group — 73 consolidated subsidiaries across warehousing, port transport, international forwarding, home-appliance 3PL, supply-chain solutions and land transport — and, of Japan's three zaibatsu-lineage warehouse majors, the one whose earnings are most purely logistics: the Logistics segment supplied 97.5% of FY3/26 external revenue and 87.0% of segment profit. Strengths: a logistics operating margin that has rebuilt from 2.1% in FY3/17 to 8.4% in FY3/26 on high-value air freight and 3PL; a second, quieter asset leg in rental real estate carried at ¥38,133mn against a fair value of ¥140,273mn, an unrealised gain of ¥102,140mn equal to about 72% of parent equity; and a February 2026 capital reset — a ¥18,748mn third-party allotment to Mitsui Fudosan alongside a buyback facility of up to ¥34,000mn — that directly addresses the share count and funds healthcare-logistics capacity. Weaknesses: return on equity of 8.6% in FY3/26 is far below the Mid-Term Plan 2022 target of more than 12%, and the plan's ¥350,000mn revenue target will be missed even after the 6 November 2026 upward revision took FY3/27 guidance to ¥330,000mn of revenue and ¥24,000mn of operating profit; real-estate profit is volatile, as the FY3/25 collapse to ¥2,161mn on the Hakozaki tenant exit showed; and no successor mid-term plan has been published, leaving the post-FY3/27 framework open. We initiate at Overweight with a 12-month target price of ¥3,800, +18.8% against the 24 November 2026 close of ¥3,199, on 20.0x our FY3/28E EPS of ¥191 (J-Core estimate). All historical financials in this report are from the company filings compiled in the J-Core financial base (tanshin and securities reports, FY3/17–FY3/26) unless stated otherwise; figures labelled J-Core estimates are our own forecasts, not company guidance.

bullets.leadHtml: The mid-term plan ends with a split scorecard
bullets.html: Mid-Term Plan 2022 closes in FY3/27 with its operating-profit target beaten — revised guidance of ¥24,000mn against a ¥23,000mn target — but its revenue target missed (¥330,000mn guided against ¥350,000mn planned) and its ROE target of more than 12% unmet at 8.6% in FY3/26. The successor plan, expected with FY3/27 results in May 2027, is the single largest medium-term catalyst and the largest disclosure gap.

bullets.leadHtml: The logistics recovery is operational, not just cyclical
bullets.html: Logistics segment profit rose to ¥24,463mn in FY3/26, an 8.4% margin, from ¥4,490mn (2.1%) in FY3/17. The FY3/26 step-up was led by high-value air-freight demand at Mitsui-Soko Express, and H1 FY3/27 delivered 50.0% of the revised full-year operating-profit guidance, with the company citing volumes above plan, new business wins and cost reductions.

bullets.leadHtml: Real estate is 2.5% of revenue and a ¥102bn balance-sheet fact
bullets.html: Rental real estate is carried at ¥38,133mn against a fair value of ¥140,273mn at FY3/26 — an unrealised gain of ¥102,140mn, or ¥1,365 per share before tax (calculated), about 72% of parent equity. Earnings from the segment are smaller and lumpier: profit recovered to ¥3,661mn in FY3/26 from ¥2,161mn in FY3/25 after the MSH Nihonbashi Hakozaki Building returned to full occupancy in Q4, and company guidance points to ¥4,500mn in FY3/27.

Mitsui Fudosan took 3,000,000 new shares and 2,250,000 treasury shares at ¥3,571 per share in a ¥18,748mn third-party allotment earmarked for Kanto and Kansai healthcare-logistics facilities, while a buyback facility of up to 5,500,000 shares / ¥34,000mn (including an ASR) ran from February to July 2026; treasury shares rose to 3,187,321 by 30 September 2026. The alliance is strategically logical and governance-relevant in equal measure — see Section 9.

Our base case applies 20.0x to FY3/28E EPS of ¥191 (J-Core estimate) for a target of ¥3,800, +18.8% versus ¥3,199, which clears our +15% Overweight threshold. The bull case (¥4,300, +34.4%) assumes the real-estate recovery completes and logistics margins hold; the bear case (¥2,560, −20.0%) assumes freight normalisation repeats the FY3/25 pattern. The scenario range is therefore 54.4 percentage points wide (−20.0% to +34.4%) — this is a name where the freight cycle, not the multiple, does most of the work.

ROE was 8.6% in FY3/26 against a plan target above 12%, and our forecasts reach only about 9–10% by FY3/28 even with the buyback shrinking the equity base. Closing that gap requires either sustained logistics margins above 8%, visible monetisation of the real-estate value, or further capital returns — none of which is yet committed in a published plan.

blocks.heading: 1. Key indicators and financial history
blocks.html:
Figure 1 sets out the ten-year record. Three phases are visible. In the first (FY3/17–FY3/20), the group was digesting the acquisition spree of the early 2010s: operating profit was only ¥5,823mn in FY3/17 and a ¥25,478mn goodwill impairment in the Logistics segment drove a net loss of ¥23,427mn that year. In the second (FY3/21–FY3/23), pandemic-era freight rates lifted operating profit to a ¥25,939mn–¥25,961mn plateau; the company's own mid-term-plan materials put the underlying, ex-windfall level for FY3/22 at about ¥17,000mn, and we treat that distinction as essential to any through-cycle judgement. In the third (FY3/24–FY3/26), freight normalised, operating profit fell to ¥17,831mn in FY3/25 — a year also hit by the Hakozaki real-estate vacancy — and then recovered to ¥22,111mn in FY3/26, up 24.0% year on year, on high-value air freight and logistics volume.

Per-share figures for FY3/22–FY3/26 are as reported, restated for the 1-for-3 share split of 1 May 2025; earlier years are shown on the same split basis as calculated from the originally reported figures, and dividends are shown as actually paid, so the dividend series is not split-adjusted for FY3/25 and earlier. Interest-bearing debt is disclosed in the tanshin only for the current and prior years; the earlier years are therefore shown as not obtained rather than reconstructed on a different basis.

figures.sourceHtml: Company tanshin, FY3/17–FY3/26, as tabulated in Figure 1 of this report.

blocks.heading: FY3/2026 in the ten-year record
blocks.html: FY3/26 revenue of ¥299,472mn rose 6.7% and operating profit of ¥22,111mn rose 24.0%; net income attributable to parent was ¥11,151mn (EPS ¥148.27) and ROE was 8.6%. The quality points matter more than the growth rates. First, non-controlling interests took ¥3,387mn of the ¥14,539mn total net profit — several operating subsidiaries are not wholly owned, a legacy of the Sony joint-venture structure — so the parent-attributable line, not total profit, is the one to capitalise. Second, the year carried ¥802mn of head-office relocation costs and ¥410mn of capital-policy costs in special losses, both connected to the February 2026 Mitsui Fudosan transaction. Third, operating cash flow of ¥23,697mn against capital expenditure of ¥9,861mn (cash basis) left the group with ¥47,698mn of cash and equivalents and interest-bearing debt of ¥85,721mn, a D/E of 0.60x on the company's own presentation.

blocks.heading: 2. Latest update — H1 FY3/2027 and the guidance revision
blocks.html: H1 FY3/27 (April–September 2026) delivered revenue of ¥165,541mn, operating profit of ¥11,992mn and net income of ¥6,770mn. On 6 November 2026 the company revised full-year guidance up: revenue to ¥330,000mn (+4.4% versus the initial forecast), operating profit to ¥24,000mn (+4.3%), net income to ¥13,000mn and EPS to ¥173.40, with the dividend raised to ¥52. H1 progress against the revised full year is 50.2% on revenue, 50.0% on operating profit and 52.1% on net income — a clean halfway profile that neither promises a further raise nor suggests slippage. The company attributes the revision to logistics volumes above plan, new business wins and site start-ups on schedule, cost-reduction measures, and a better non-operating balance. H1 also included a ¥600mn gain on the transfer of the insurance-agency business of Mitsui-Soko Bizport, booked in special profit; it supports net income but not operating profit, and our forecasts treat it as non-recurring.

blocks.heading: 3. Business description
blocks.html: Mitsui-Soko traces its origin to 1909, when it was spun out of Mitsui Bank's warehouse department as Higashijin Soko; it adopted the holding-company structure in 2014. The parent company runs group management and the real-estate business, and five operating companies run the logistics businesses inside the single reported Logistics segment. The group comprised 74 subsidiaries and 6 affiliates at FY3/26, with 7,654 consolidated employees; FY3/26 revenue split ¥215,937mn in Japan and ¥83,535mn in other regions.

blocks.heading: Group structure — a holding company over five operating companies
blocks.html: Mitsui-Soko Co., Ltd. is the core warehousing, cargo-handling and port-transport company and runs the overseas logistics network. Mitsui-Soko Express is the international forwarder — air freight and multimodal transport — built from the JTB cargo group acquired in 2011; it was the unit behind the FY3/26 air-freight earnings step-up. Mitsui-Soko Logistics runs home-appliance logistics and 3PL on a shared-platform model; it originated as Sanyo Electric Logistics, consolidated in 2012 — the home-appliance logistics M&A that gave the group its largest domestic 3PL franchise. Mitsui-Soko Supply Chain Solutions (MSCSS) provides procurement, in-plant and sales-logistics support built on electronics know-how; it originated as Sony's logistics arm, transferred to a Sony/Mitsui-Soko joint venture in April 2015. Mitsui-Soko Transport, established in November 2015, runs the nationwide land-freight network and absorbed the Marukyo transport group in December 2015. These five are management units inside one reportable segment; the segment disclosure, not the company structure, is what the P&L shows.

blocks.heading: What the logistics business actually does
blocks.html: By revenue type in FY3/26, transport income was ¥143,766mn — the largest line — followed by warehouse handling fees of ¥42,155mn, storage fees of ¥39,990mn, port operations of ¥17,211mn, real-estate income of ¥7,509mn and other income of ¥48,839mn. The mix explains the earnings character: this is not a rent-collecting warehouse landlord with a logistics sideline, but a transport- and handling-weighted operator whose storage base provides the stable core. The growth agenda in the current plan is healthcare logistics — the use of proceeds of the Mitsui Fudosan allotment is ¥11,366mn for a Kanto healthcare facility and ¥7,000mn for a Kansai one — alongside 3PL and supply-chain work where the Sanyo and Sony heritages give it manufacturer-side credibility that pure warehouse operators do not have.

blocks.heading: 4. Market and value chain
blocks.html:
The industry frame is value-led, not volume-led. Yano Research Institute (press release of 5 August 2026) puts Japan's 15-sector logistics market at ¥24.794tn in FY2024 (+5.7%) and forecasts ¥25.360tn in FY2025 (+2.3%) and ¥26.361tn in FY2026 (+3.9%) — growth of roughly +2–4% a year in yen terms, which Yano attributes mainly to freight, storage and handling rate revisions and exchange rates rather than to a full recovery in freight volume. Third-party estimates of Japan 3PL growth cluster around +4–5.5% a year (IMARC Group: 4.3% CAGR 2025–33; Expert Market Research: 5.4% CAGR 2025–34, on different and mutually inconsistent market definitions — we cite the range, not an average). MLIT's physical series agree with the value-led reading: ordinary-warehouse storage balances are rising about 2% a year while throughput is broadly flat. Figure 3 maps where Mitsui-Soko sits in that chain: an integrated operator spanning storage, handling, 3PL and forwarding, with the real-estate business sitting alongside the chain rather than inside it.

The structural drivers are labour scarcity and price pass-through. The April 2024 truck-driver overtime cap institutionalised rate revisions and itemised waiting and handling charges; the warehouse sector's own storage-fee index had been broadly flat since 2000 even as construction costs rose, so warehousing price catch-up is earlier-stage and less certain than trucking's. For Mitsui-Soko, the investment question is whether its 8.4% logistics margin can be held as the 2024-problem repricing annualises — our base case assumes it fades only gradually, because the 3PL and healthcare mix is still improving.

blocks.heading: Competitor positioning
blocks.html: Figure 4 compares the three zaibatsu-lineage majors and Kamigumi on reported FY3/26 figures and 24 November 2026 prices. The contrast is instructive. Mitsubishi Logistics (9301) is the real-estate-heavy name: real estate supplied about half of its two segments' combined operating profit, and its FY3/26 EPS of ¥155.84 is heavily flattered by ¥67,281mn of investment-securities sale gains, so its 8.0x trailing P/E is not a clean earnings multiple. Sumitomo Warehouse (9303) trades at 0.93x book with a 16.6x P/E — the balance-sheet-value end of the group, carrying a large policy-shareholding portfolio. Kamigumi (9364), Japan's largest port operator, is the sector's largest company by market capitalisation at ¥519,562mn (Nikkei, 24 November 2026); its reported financials were not part of the sourced base for this report and are not shown. Mitsui-Soko is the mirror image of Mitsubishi Logistics: the most logistics-pure earnings mix of the three, the highest P/B at 1.73x, and a trailing P/E of 21.6x that falls to 16.7x on our FY3/28E EPS. The market is already paying for the logistics purity; what it is not yet paying for, in our view, is the combination of the real-estate fair value and a completed capital reset.

blocks.heading: 5. Segments and real estate
blocks.html:
The group has reported the same two segments for the entire ten-year window — Logistics and Real estate — with no reorganisation, which makes Figure 5 a genuinely consistent series. Logistics earned ¥24,463mn on ¥291,963mn of external revenue in FY3/26 (8.4% margin); corporate adjustments of −¥6,013mn, mainly holding-company management costs, reconcile segment profit to consolidated operating profit of ¥22,111mn. The corporate cost line has grown from −¥3,673mn in FY3/17 to −¥6,013mn and is a quiet drag that any margin bridge must carry.

The real-estate segment's profit history is the volatility exhibit: about ¥5.0–5.9bn a year through FY3/24, then ¥2,161mn in FY3/25 when a major tenant partially vacated the MSH Nihonbashi Hakozaki Building and occupancy fell into the 60% range during its conversion to multi-tenant use, then ¥3,661mn in FY3/26 as full occupancy was restored in Q4. Even restored, the profit is below the pre-2025 level because the multi-tenant cost structure is heavier; we therefore treat the company's ¥4,500mn FY3/27 segment guidance as the recovery path, not a return to ¥5.9bn.

blocks.heading: Rental real estate — the hidden-asset leg
blocks.html: Figure 7 shows the disclosure that anchors the asset story. Rental real estate was carried at ¥38,133mn at FY3/26 against a fair value of ¥140,273mn — fair values are based on external appraisals for major properties and internal income-capitalisation calculations for others — leaving an unrealised gain of ¥102,140mn, up from ¥92,804mn a year earlier. That is ¥1,365 per share before tax (calculated on 74,803,785 shares ex-treasury), or about ¥956 per share after a notional 30% tax, which would lift BPS from ¥1,849.68 to about ¥2,805 on an adjusted basis; the share price of ¥3,199 is 1.14x that adjusted figure, against 1.73x reported book. Two cautions apply. The gain is a valuation fact, not an earnings stream: rental profit booked in operating profit was ¥3,433mn in FY3/26. And the FY3/26 book-value increase of ¥8,154mn mainly reflected a rise in the rental-use proportion of properties, so part of the fair-value uplift is reclassification as much as market appreciation.

blocks.heading: 6. Financial statements summary
blocks.html: The balance sheet at FY3/26 showed total assets of ¥310,706mn, net assets of ¥157,093mn and an equity ratio of 45.7%. Segment assets were ¥199,464mn in Logistics, ¥39,221mn in Real estate and ¥72,021mn of corporate assets. Depreciation of ¥11,406mn split ¥5,153mn Logistics, ¥1,883mn Real estate and ¥4,370mn corporate — the corporate share, which includes the head-office building, is unusually large and is part of why the adjustment line in Figure 5 is what it is.

blocks.heading: Balance sheet and cash flow
blocks.html: Operating cash flow has been stable in a ¥21–24bn band since FY3/24 (¥23,697mn in FY3/26), below the mid-term plan's ¥30,000mn ambition for the plan's final year. Cash capital expenditure was ¥9,861mn in FY3/26 (¥13,304mn on the accrual basis of the segment note). The February 2026 transactions changed the shape of the balance sheet more than a year of trading did: ¥18,366mn of net allotment proceeds came in, the buyback then spent ¥8,641mn in H1 FY3/27 alone, and cash and equivalents stood at ¥43,854mn at September 2026 against interest-bearing debt of ¥87,514mn. Leverage is not the constraint on this story — D/E was 0.60x at FY3/26 against a plan discipline of about 1.0x — which is precisely why the ROE debate in Section 9 is about asset and capital efficiency, not solvency.

blocks.heading: 7. J-Core forecasts
blocks.html: Figure 8 bridges from the company's revised guidance to our estimates. For FY3/27, the J-Core estimate sits fractionally above guidance — revenue ¥331,000mn, operating profit ¥24,300mn, net income ¥13,200mn, EPS ¥176 — on three grounds: H1 progress is at or slightly above the halfway mark on every line; the initial (May 2026) segment guidance already pointed to ¥4,500mn of real-estate profit on the completed occupancy recovery, and the November revision did not walk that back; and the ¥600mn Bizport transfer gain supports the net line. We do not assume a further guidance raise. For FY3/28, we forecast revenue of ¥344,000mn (+3.9%, in line with the Yano industry range plus modest share gain in healthcare and 3PL), operating profit of ¥26,000mn and net income of ¥14,300mn (EPS ¥191). The explicit assumptions are: (i) the Logistics margin improves from 8.4% toward 8.7% as rate revisions hold and healthcare facilities ramp, with segment profit of about ¥26,700mn; (ii) Real estate profit recovers to ¥5,000mn, still below the pre-2025 level, on a full year of full Hakozaki occupancy; (iii) corporate costs rise to about ¥5,700mn in absolute terms but fall as a share of segment profit; and (iv) the share count stays at about 74.8mn — the buyback facility closed in July 2026 and we assume no new programme until a successor plan is published. All figures in this section and Figure 8 are J-Core estimates, not company guidance.

blocks.heading: 8. Valuation and scenarios
blocks.html: Our primary method is a P/E on J-Core FY3/28E EPS, cross-checked against P/B–ROE and the real-estate-adjusted book value. The base case applies 20.0x to FY3/28E EPS of ¥191 — a premium to Sumitomo Warehouse's 16.6x trailing multiple that we justify by Mitsui-Soko's higher logistics purity and margin trajectory, and a discount to its own 21.6x trailing multiple — giving ¥3,820, rounded to a target price of ¥3,800. At ¥3,800 the shares would trade at about 1.9x our FY3/27E book value per share of roughly ¥2,024 against a forecast ROE of about 9%; on a strict P/B–ROE frame that is full, and we say so — the Overweight rests on the earnings trajectory plus the 1.14x multiple of real-estate-adjusted book, not on book-value cheapness. Figure 9 sets out the three scenarios. Bull (¥4,300, +34.4%): FY3/28 operating profit of ¥27,500mn with real-estate profit at ¥5,500mn and the logistics margin at 9.0%, EPS of ¥205 at 21.0x. Base (¥3,800, +18.8%): as Section 7. Bear (¥2,560, −20.0%): freight normalisation repeats FY3/25, operating profit falls to ¥22,500mn, real-estate profit stalls at ¥3,500mn, EPS of ¥160 at 16.0x. The stated range is −20.0% to +34.4%, a width of 54.4 percentage points. Ratings follow the pilot thresholds on the base case, 12-month horizon: Overweight at +15% or more, Neutral between −10% and +15%, Underweight at −10% or less; the base case's +18.8% gives Overweight.

blocks.heading: 9. Risks, management and strategy
blocks.html:
Risks to our view. (1) ROE delivery: the plan target of more than 12% was missed by a wide margin (8.6% in FY3/26) and our forecasts do not close the gap; if the successor plan again promises more than the P&L delivers, the P/B premium to peers compresses. (2) The missing plan: no successor to Mid-Term Plan 2022 had been published as of 24 November 2026, so capital allocation beyond the completed buyback — including whether the real-estate value is ever surfaced — is uncommitted management discretion. (3) The Mitsui Fudosan relationship: the alliance brings healthcare-logistics deal flow and a credible property partner, but a roughly 7% anchor shareholder with board-level strategic overlap also raises the standard questions about related-party facility transactions and about whether real-estate value will be realised for all shareholders or within the alliance. (4) Real-estate earnings volatility: FY3/25 showed that a single building's tenant exit can remove ¥3.8bn of segment profit in a year; the portfolio is concentrated in a small number of office buildings. (5) Freight cyclicality: the FY3/22–23 windfall and the FY3/24–25 fade are both in the ten-year record; air-freight rates are the swing factor in the Express business. (6) Cost pass-through: the sector's storage and handling price catch-up is incomplete, and wage inflation in a labour-short industry is structural.

On strategy, management's record is genuinely two-sided. The operating build of the past decade — Sanyo, Sony and Marukyo integrations inside one segment, margin repair from 2.1% to 8.4% — is strong. The capital record is newer: the Mitsui Fudosan allotment and the ¥34bn buyback are the first decisive moves on a balance sheet that carries ¥102bn of unrealised real-estate gains and a 45.7% equity ratio. What we monitor next: the successor plan's ROE and capital-return language (expected May 2027), quarterly logistics margin against the 8.4% FY3/26 base, Hakozaki occupancy and the real-estate profit run-rate against the ¥4,500mn FY3/27 guide, and any further treasury-share cancellation or buyback authorisation.

blocks.heading: 10. Basis of preparation
blocks.html: Sources: FY3/2026 tanshin (13 May 2026) and H1 FY3/2027 tanshin (6 November 2026) via JPX/TDnet; FY3/2026 securities report (filed 22 June 2026); the 6 February 2026 Mitsui Fudosan alliance and allotment releases; company IR materials for the mid-term plan and group structure; Yano Research Institute logistics-market press release of 5 August 2026 and IMARC / Expert Market Research 3PL estimates for industry context (each forecast is labelled with its owner in Section 4); peer figures from the 9301 and 9303 J-Core financial bases (reported FY3/26 figures and 24 November 2026 prices) and Kamigumi's market capitalisation from Nikkei company data as compiled in the J-Core sector universe (24 November 2026). Share price: ¥3,199, close of 24 November 2026 (Finnhub market data — a secondary market source; no primary source exists for prices). Forecasts labelled J-Core estimates are ours; company figures are labelled reported or guidance at first use. Gaps, stated honestly: BPS for FY3/17, FY3/18 and FY3/21 was not obtained; interest-bearing debt before FY3/25 is not disclosed on a consistent basis and is shown as not obtained; rental-real-estate fair values before FY3/25 were not extracted; segment figures for FY3/17–FY3/24 rest on an XBRL compilation of the securities reports whose FY3/25–26 overlap agrees exactly with the primary tanshin; the revised FY3/27 segment profit split was not obtained (the initial May 2026 split is used); and FY3/18's dividend as compiled in the secondary series (nil) was not primary-verified. This report is for information only and is not investment advice or a solicitation.
